# 2026 Paycheck & Take-Home Pay Calculator Guide: How Much of Your Salary You Actually Keep

Nobody opens their first pay stub expecting the number at the bottom to feel smaller than the number they were promised in the offer letter. Yet that gap — between gross salary and net, spendable income — is exactly where most people get caught off guard. Federal income tax, FICA, state income tax, and pre-tax deductions all take a bite before your paycheck ever reaches your bank account, and the size of each bite depends on where you live, how you're paid, and how you fill out your W-4.

This guide walks through every piece of that puzzle for the 2026 tax year, using the latest IRS brackets, Social Security wage base, and standard deduction figures. Along the way, you'll find worked examples, state-by-state comparisons, and answers to the questions people most often ask when they're trying to figure out what a job offer is actually worth.

For an instant calculation based on your specific situation, you can use our [free 2026 paycheck calculator](/paycheck-calculator) which covers all 50 states and is updated for OBBBA changes.

## 1. What Determines Your Take-Home Pay

Take-home pay, also called net pay, is what's left of your gross salary after every mandatory and elected deduction is subtracted. Four categories of deductions typically apply to a W-2 employee:

- **Federal income tax** — a progressive tax calculated using IRS brackets and your filing status
- **FICA taxes** — a flat-rate combination of Social Security and Medicare
- **State (and sometimes local) income tax** — which varies enormously depending on where you live and work
- **Pre-tax and post-tax deductions** — such as 401(k) contributions, health insurance premiums, and HSA contributions

Because state tax rules differ so widely, two people earning identical salaries can end up with take-home pay that differs by thousands of dollars a year purely based on their zip code. That's the single biggest reason a generic paycheck calculator isn't enough — you need to understand how each layer stacks on top of the others.

## 2. 2026 Federal Income Tax Brackets

The IRS adjusts its tax brackets every year for inflation, and 2026 brought a slightly larger-than-usual adjustment tied to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which made most 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act provisions permanent. There are still seven federal tax rates in 2026 — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37%.

| Rate | Single Filers | Married Filing Jointly | Head of Household |
|------|---------------|------------------------|--------------------|
| 10% | $0 – $11,925 | $0 – $23,850 | $0 – $17,000 |
| 12% | $11,925 – $47,750 | $23,850 – $95,500 | $17,000 – $64,850 |
| 22% | $47,750 – $100,525 | $95,500 – $201,050 | $64,850 – $103,350 |
| 24% | $100,525 – $191,950 | $201,050 – $383,900 | $103,350 – $197,300 |
| 32% | $191,950 – $243,725 | $383,900 – $487,450 | $197,300 – $250,500 |
| 35% | $243,725 – $609,350 | $487,450 – $731,200 | $250,500 – $609,350 |
| 37% | $609,350+ | $731,200+ | $609,350+ |

*Source: Tax Foundation, 2026 Tax Brackets, based on IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-25. For a deeper dive, see our complete [2026 federal tax brackets guide](/federal-tax-brackets).*

Remember that these are **marginal** rates. Only the income that falls inside a given bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate — moving into a higher bracket never reduces your take-home pay on the dollars you already earned.

**2026 standard deduction:**

- Single: $16,100
- Married Filing Jointly: $32,200
- Head of Household: $24,150

## 3. FICA Taxes: Social Security and Medicare in 2026

FICA — the Federal Insurance Contributions Act — funds Social Security and Medicare, and it's charged at a flat rate regardless of your income level.

The Social Security portion (OASDI) is 6.2% on earnings up to the applicable taxable maximum, while the Medicare portion (HI) is 1.45% on all earnings with no cap. Combined, that's the familiar 7.65% FICA rate you'll see withheld from every paycheck.

For 2026, the Social Security wage base is $184,500, an increase of $8,400 from $176,100 in 2025 — pushing the maximum Social Security tax an employee will pay for the year up to $11,439.

**Quick FICA reference for 2026:**

| Component | Rate | Wage Cap |
|-----------|------|----------|
| Social Security | 6.2% (employee) + 6.2% (employer) | $184,500 |
| Medicare | 1.45% (employee) + 1.45% (employer) | No cap |
| Additional Medicare Tax | 0.9% (employee only) | Applies above $200K single / $250K MFJ |

Self-employed individuals pay both the employee and employer share — 15.3% total — though half of that is deductible against income tax. Use our [self-employment tax calculator](/self-employment-tax-calculator) to estimate your SE tax liability.

## 4. State Income Tax: The Variable That Changes Everything

Federal tax and FICA are identical no matter where you live. State tax is where paychecks diverge dramatically, and it's the piece most generic calculators oversimplify.

States generally fall into three buckets:

- **No state income tax:** Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming.
- **Flat-rate states:** States like Pennsylvania (3.07%), Illinois (4.95%), Colorado (4.4%), and Michigan (4.25%).
- **Progressive-bracket states:** States like California (1%–13.3%), New York (4%–10.9%), and Minnesota (5.35%–9.85%).

Our state-specific guides for [California](/california-tax-calculator), [Texas](/texas-tax-calculator), [Florida](/florida-tax-calculator), [New York](/new-york-tax-calculator), and [Illinois](/illinois-tax-calculator) break this down in detail.

## 5. Step-by-Step: How to Calculate Your Net Pay

Here's the general formula that every paycheck calculator, including the fanciest ones, is ultimately running behind the scenes:

1. **Start with gross pay** — your salary or hourly wage times hours worked.
2. **Subtract pre-tax deductions** — 401(k) contributions, HSA/FSA contributions, and pre-tax health insurance premiums.
3. **Calculate federal withholding** — apply the standard deduction, then run the remainder through the 2026 tax brackets.
4. **Calculate FICA** — apply 6.2% Social Security (up to $184,500 cap) and 1.45% Medicare.
5. **Calculate state and local tax** — using your state's specific brackets, flat rate, or exemption.
6. **Subtract post-tax deductions** — Roth 401(k) contributions, wage garnishments, or after-tax insurance premiums.
7. **What's left is your net (take-home) pay.**

Doing this by hand for every pay period is tedious, which is exactly why [online paycheck calculators](/paycheck-calculator) exist.

## 6. Worked Example: $75,000 Salary in Three States

To show how dramatically location changes the outcome, here's the same $75,000 salary (single filer, standard deduction, no pre-tax deductions) run through three different states using 2026 rates.

**Texas (no state income tax):**
- Federal tax: approximately $7,670
- FICA: $5,737.50
- State tax: $0
- **Estimated net pay: ~$61,590**

**Illinois (4.95% flat tax):**
- Federal tax: approximately $7,670
- FICA: $5,737.50
- State tax: approximately $3,575
- **Estimated net pay: ~$58,020**

**California (progressive, 1%–13.3%):**
- Federal tax: approximately $7,670
- FICA: $5,737.50
- State tax: approximately $2,640
- **Estimated net pay: ~$59,000**

The spread between the highest and lowest outcome is roughly $3,500 a year — on an identical salary.

## 7. Pre-Tax Deductions That Lower Your Taxable Income

One of the most underused levers for increasing take-home pay isn't a raise — it's reducing taxable income legally through pre-tax benefits:

- **401(k) or 403(b) contributions:** For 2026, the employee contribution limit is $23,500.
- **Health Savings Account (HSA):** Up to $4,300 (self) or $8,550 (family) in 2026.
- **Flexible Spending Account (FSA):** Up to $3,300 in 2026.
- **Traditional IRA contributions:** Up to $7,000, subject to income limits.

## 8. Overtime, Bonuses, and Supplemental Wages

Bonuses are often withheld at a flat 22% federal supplemental rate. Overtime pay under OBBBA may be eligible for a new temporary federal deduction through 2028. See our [overtime tax calculator](/overtime-tax-calculator) for details.

## 9. Self-Employed and 1099 Workers: A Different Formula

If you're a freelancer, gig worker, or independent contractor, your paycheck math looks different:

- **Self-employment tax:** You owe the full 15.3% FICA equivalent yourself.
- **Quarterly estimated payments:** The IRS expects estimated tax payments four times a year.
- **Business deductions:** Home office, mileage, equipment, and health insurance can reduce taxable income.

## 10. How to Adjust Your Withholding (W-4)

Your Form W-4 tells your employer how much federal tax to withhold from each paycheck. Use our [IRS withholding calculator](/irs-withholding-calculator) to estimate the right withholding amount.

## 11. Common Take-Home Pay Mistakes to Avoid

- **Ignoring local taxes** — Cities like NYC levy their own income tax.
- **Comparing gross salaries across states without adjusting for tax.**
- **Assuming a big refund is "free money."** — A large refund means too much was withheld.
- **Not revisiting withholding after a raise or bonus year.**

## 12. Frequently Asked Questions

**Is take-home pay the same as net pay?**
Yes. "Take-home pay" and "net pay" are used interchangeably.

**Why did my paycheck get bigger later in the year?**
Once your year-to-date earnings pass the Social Security wage base ($184,500 in 2026), the 6.2% Social Security withholding stops for the rest of the year.

**Does bonus income get taxed at a higher rate than regular pay?**
Not permanently. Bonuses are often withheld at a flat 22% rate, but your actual tax liability is reconciled when you file.

**Do I pay state tax where I live or where I work?**
Generally, you owe tax to the state where the work is physically performed.

**How much should I contribute to my 401(k) to lower my tax bracket?**
Contributing enough to capture a full employer match is almost always worthwhile.

**Are 2026 tax brackets higher or lower than 2025?**
Slightly higher in dollar terms due to annual inflation indexing plus OBBBA adjustments.

---

### Key Takeaways

Your paycheck is the product of several independent systems — federal brackets, a flat-rate FICA system with a rising wage base, and a patchwork of state rules — all layered on top of your gross salary. Understanding each layer, rather than treating your paycheck as a black box, puts you in a much better position to negotiate offers, plan a relocation, adjust your withholding, and avoid unpleasant surprises at tax time.
